title: Optimization in offshore supply vessel planning
Offshore supply vessel chartering
Fuzzy Logic Controller for Dynamic Positioning of an Offshore Supply Vessel
abstract: The purpose of this paper is to examine the performance of fuzzy controller applied to a dynamic positioning system of ship by numerical simulation. By definition, dynamic positioning system is computer controlled system which uses the active thrusters to automatically maintain the position and heading of the ship. The proposed control scheme consist of low pass filter in cascade with three proportional derivative type fuzzy controller with Mamdani type inference scheme. Feed-forward compensation decoupling scheme is employed to reduce coupling between sway and yaw. Robustness of control scheme is assessed for Cybership II in presence of wave disturbances.

title: Assessment of Current Offshore Supply Vessel Capabilities for Crew Transfer Operations in the Flemish Pass
abstract: The Flemish Pass is a region off the coast of the province of Newfoundland and Labrador in which large oil discoveries have been made in recent years, making it a promising site for future offshore oil and gas developments. The site is located approximately 200 kilometers North-East of the currently producing Jeanne D’Arc Basin. This results in some additional challenges, including: higher waves and rougher seas on average, longer transit time from shore to any potential production facilities, and an increased risk of sea ice. Crew transfers from Offshore Supply Vessels (OSVs) to current production platforms offshore Newfoundland and Labrador are typically accomplished with a FROG-6 personnel-transfer capsule lifted by a platform-board crane. In current practice, for fixed platforms, this is only done when there is a Significant Wave Height (Hs) of 4.0 m or less, regardless of the OSV being used. In the winter months, this general-purpose approach does not allow for an acceptably high operational fraction of time in which crew transfers could be completed in the Flemish Pass. The FROG-6 capsule has designated operational limits based on the relative velocity between the capsule and the vessel deck, which will vary based on ship size, loading condition, and sea-state. Considering this, a series of geometrically similar OSV hull forms are created to represent the range of currently operating vessels. The developed models are between 70.0–90.0 m long, have a maximum breadth between 17.0–22.0 m, and block coefficients ranging from 0.65–0.79. Using ShipMo3D, a potential flow / panel code seakeeping solver, a 20 minute time history of ship motions is determined for all the modelled OSVs, across the range of sea-states realistically expected in the Flemish Pass. Then, a MATLAB script is used to transform these motions into deck velocities. From these results, the operational limits for crew transfer can be re-defined as a function of ship size, loading condition, and sea-state. This results in higher operability percentages than those achieved from using the flat wave height limit alone, with relatively large variations between differently sized and loaded ships. Further work must be done to officially implement new limits, such as: analysis of additional wave period and height combinations, further analysis of the time between limit exceedances, computational fluid dynamics simulations, “smart crane” modelling, and/or full scale sea trials.

title: Offshore Supply Vessels
AI-Driven CAPEX Forecasting for Resilient Energy Supply Chains: Integrating Offshore Project Planning with Supply Chain Risk Analytics
abstract: The global energy sector faces unprecedented volatility, where capital expenditure (CAPEX) overruns and supply chain disruptions threaten the viability of offshore projects. Traditional forecasting methods, reliant on deterministic models and static contingency, have proven inadequate, with mega-projects exceeding budgets by 30-50% on average. This article presents a transformative framework integrating Artificial Intelligence (AI)driven forecasting with supply chain risk analytics to enhance resilience in energy supply chains. Drawing on Maheshwari's (2025) pioneering work on AI-driven CAPEX forecasting for offshore oil projects, the proposed Resilient CAPEX Planning Engine (RCPE) framework combines probabilistic forecasting, digital twin simulation, and real-time risk intelligence. The framework enables organizations to move from reactive risk management to proactive, data-driven resilience building supply chains capable of not only of withstanding disruption but also of learning and strengthening through it. This article synthesizes contemporary literature to provide a practical roadmap for energy firms seeking to transform project planning and execution in an era of deep uncertainty.

title: AI-Optimized Offshore Supply Vessel Operations for Fuel Efficiency, Emissions Reduction, and Operational Sustainability
abstract: Abstract This paper investigates the application of AI-driven optimisation to offshore supply vessel (OSV) operations in order to reduce fuel consumption, minimise emissions, and improve logistical efficiency in offshore oil and gas activities. The objective is to develop an intelligent operational framework capable of dynamically optimising vessel routing, speed profiles, and load distribution based on real-time environmental and operational conditions. An integrated optimisation framework was developed using operational vessel data, meteorological conditions, wave parameters, fuel consumption profiles, and offshore scheduling requirements. Machine learning and predictive routing algorithms were applied to continuously evaluate optimal navigation paths, vessel speeds, and cargo allocation strategies under varying offshore conditions. A real-time optimisation model was designed to dynamically respond to weather fluctuations, operational delays, and changing supply demands. Simulation studies were conducted using representative offshore logistics scenarios to evaluate fuel efficiency, emissions reduction, voyage reliability, and operational responsiveness. Comparative benchmarking was performed against conventional fixed-route offshore supply operations. Simulation studies indicate that the proposed AI-optimised framework has the potential to reduce offshore vessel fuel consumption by approximately 16% compared to conventional operations. These results, while promising, are derived from discrete-event simulation and require validation through real-world deployment. The framework demonstrates pathway viability for achieving measurable efficiency gains, with simulation suggesting proportional CO2 emissions reductions and improved voyage scheduling performance. Dynamic route optimisation enabled vessels to avoid high-resistance sea conditions, reducing unnecessary engine loading and improving overall energy efficiency. Adaptive speed control further contributed to fuel savings while maintaining operational delivery requirements.The system also demonstrated improved responsiveness to operational disruptions, including weather-related delays and fluctuating offshore demand schedules. AI-assisted cargo allocation reduced inefficient load distribution and minimised unnecessary vessel movements between offshore facilities. Comparative analysis indicates that the proposed framework outperforms traditional fixed-routing strategies in both environmental and operational performance metrics.In addition to reducing operating costs, the framework supports offshore sustainability objectives by lowering fuel usage and enhancing logistical coordination across offshore assets. The findings demonstrate strong potential for integrating AI-driven optimisation into offshore marine operations as part of broader digital transformation and decarbonization initiatives within the upstream energy sector. This work introduces a real-time, AI-assisted optimisation framework specifically designed for offshore supply vessel operations in the upstream sector. Unlike conventional marine logistics approaches based on static routing and scheduling, the proposed system integrates environmental data, operational demand, and predictive optimisation to simultaneously enhance fuel efficiency, reduce emissions, and improve offshore logistical performance within a scalable digital operations framework.

title: A probabilistic approach to determine design loads for collision between an offshore supply vessel and offshore installations
Vertical Motions Assessment of an Offshore Supply Vessel in Concept Design Stage
venue: Technology and Science for the Ships of the Future
abstract: The main hydrodynamic characteristics of an Offshore Vessel are mostly referring to motion behaviour in rough sea. For such kind of ships, good seakeeping performances are mandatory, and, besides dynamic positioning quality, maybe more relevant than purely propulsive issues. The seakeeping performances of a ship are strongly influenced by main geometric parameters selected since concept design stage. Means that, to improve the designers' ability to properly select the best preferred design, enhanced methods should be implemented in such a way to accurately determine seakeeping performances as function of the more significant geometrical parameters and non-dimensional ratios. In the present work a procedure, based on the determination of multiple regression models with different parameter combinations, has been developed to reproduce the vertical motions transfer functions of a generic supply vessel at different encounter angles and operational speeds. The regressions have been obtained from 2D strip theory calculations on a family of supply vessels, ensuring a sufficiently accurate estimate of heave and pitch motions since concept design stage. Besides, the transfer functions have been also determined with the application of a trained neural network and the results have been compared with regressions outcomes on a reference hull.

title: A Feature-rich Offshore Supply Vessel Routing and Scheduling Problem in the Oil and Gas Industry
abstract: This paper addresses a routing and scheduling problem for supply vessels that service multiple offshore facilities from a central base. The problem incorporates various operational requirements, such as the use of a heterogeneous fleet, split deliveries, multiple visits to each facility, time windows with allowed service interruptions due to facility closing hours, and berth capacity. The aim is to prepare a 7-day schedule for each vessel that will be repeated each week to minimise the total operational cost and fixed cost of chartering vessels. We formulate the problem as a mixed-integer programming (MILP) model that determines fleet composition, vessel routing, service timing, and delivery quantities. Building on this MILP, we propose a matheuristic based on a multi-start iterated local search framework. The heuristic explores neighbourhoods associated with fleet composition and routing decisions. For a given fleet composition and routing decision, a simplified formulation is derived by fixing the corresponding fleet composition and routing decisions in MILP. The simplified formulation is solved for optimal timing and quantity decisions. We also introduce a benchmark dataset constructed using the operational data of a leading Australian oil and gas company. Computational experiments show that the proposed heuristic effectively produces high‑quality solutions for these benchmark instances.

title: How the First Jones Act Compliant Wind Turbine Installation Vessel is Helping to Develop the U.S. Offshore Wind Supply Chain
abstract: Abstract Meeting the U.S. offshore wind target of 30 GW installed capacity by 2030 will present significant supply chain opportunities for port infrastructure developments, major windfarm components, increased steel demand, and construction of transportation and installation (T&I) solutions in U.S. shipyards such as specialized wind turbine installation vessels (WTIVs). This paper discusses how the design and construction of "Charybdis" –– the first Jones Act Compliant WTIV –– are helping to drive the supply chain for offshore wind development and the energy transition toward more sustainable solutions. A consortium of designer and shipyard led by a major developer, Dominion Energy is building the Charybdis WTIV. This paper highlights how the project team leveraged experience in the oil and gas industry and offshore wind from Europe to develop the first specialized WTIV for U.S. wind farm construction and East Coast operation. The paper also discusses important aspects such as project execution, risk assessment, technology innovation, and compliance with U.S. Regulations and safety standards. The Charybdis is one of the largest WTIVs in the world and an important enabler for a safer and more cost-effective deployment of U.S. offshore wind energy and a move toward sustainable energy solutions. The insights and experience gained with the concept development, design, and construction of Charybdis, will benefit the next generation turbine installations in the U.S. and worldwide, and promote the collaboration of future wind turbine supply chain development.

title: Resolving Offshore EPCI Supply-Chain Disruption Through Integrated Marine Logistics Planning and Contractual Backcharge Governance
abstract: Abstract Offshore engineering, procurement, construction, and installation projects can carry substantial marine cost even when the nominal vessel spread is adequate. The problem is usually not a simple shortage of barges, landing craft, or tugs. It is the loss of control between cargo demand, physical readiness, berth access, towage approvals, project ownership, fuel and freshwater transfers, standby causation, and the records needed for commercial recovery. This paper describes a marine-logistics governance pilot developed for concurrent offshore-island construction work. The pilot ran over a 16-week operating window and treated each voyage as both an operational movement and a project-controls event. A daily cargo cut-off, readiness gate, critical-path review, voyage sanction, cause-code library, fuel and water allocation hierarchy, evidence-completeness check, and exception dashboard were brought together through a Voyage Accountability Ledger. The operating sample covered 181 cargo requests, 71 cargo-barge and landing-craft voyages, 84 crew-boat movements, 20 towage-approval cycles, 55 fuel or freshwater transfers, and 32 delay or standby events. The pilot improved requests received before cut-off from 43% to 94%, complete project/package ownership from 57% to 99%, and complete voyage-ledger coverage from 14% to 98%. Low-utilisation sailings below 50% of practical deck area fell from 63% to 10%. Events classified within 24 hours increased from 34% to 96%, while unidentified standby reduced from 31% to 3%. Fuel and freshwater recovery-record completeness increased from 49% to 98%, and the median time needed to assemble a backcharge evidence pack reduced from 5.9 days to 0.6 days. The results show that marine logistics can be governed as one connected operating and commercial process, improving planning discipline, shared-berth coordination, cost allocation, and the quality of claims and backcharges.

title: Real-Time Offshore Supply Vessel Routing Problem with Random Service Requests
venue: Journal of Engineering Research and Reports
abstract: The routing of supply vessels to offshore platforms is one of the major tasks in upstream logistics planning in the oil and gas industry. This task involves the formulation and solution of a real-time variant of the stochastic dynamic vehicle routing problem, which reflects the operational environment of offshore platforms in practice. In this paper, a novel mixed integer linear programming-based heuristic is presented with a view to determining the optimal route of a single supply vessel allocated to provide service to a group of offshore platforms through the supply of spare parts, liquid bulk liquids, and other materials, allowing for random service requests by the offshore platform group. The proposed heuristic is applied to a real-world case study of vessel routing to offshore platforms in the South Atlantic Ocean Shelf. The computational performance of the heuristic, as assessed by the degree of dynamism, is found to be very good.

Assessment of Station Keeping Capability for Dynamically Positioned Offshore Supply Vessel
venue: Journal of Ship Production and Design
abstract: Abstract Dynamic positioning capability (DPCap) assessment is essential during the preliminary investigation of the positioning ability of a newly designed dynamic positioning system (DPS). Operational safety is always the first consideration in the design and operation of a new DPS. To be able to plan a safe and efficient operation, it is important to know the maximum environmental conditions that the DP vessel can withstand. The main objective of this article is to present a developed tool capable of conducting the DPCap analysis for offshore supply vessels based on the DNVGL methodology. The article describes the background studies, methodology, and mechanism associated with the formulation and development of the tool. The optimization of the design variables for the station-keeping criteria targets the highest capability at the lowest possible energy expenditure. Finally, the results are presented in the form of standard capability polar plots to show the application of the computational assessment procedure. The accuracy and reliability of the DPCap tool are validated by comparing with the results of the commercial one for the same case study ship at multiple simulation cases. Introduction Many offshore operations require the vessel to be kept in a position to face environmental loads from wind, waves and current. This can be achieved using Dynamic Positioning System (DPS) by using thrusters (Sørensen 2011). Station keeping ability is used in different types of vessels with varying operational requirements. Cruise vessels and mega yachts use it in the form of virtual anchoring to avoid the environmental impact of anchoring in the sensitive estuaries they often ply. The importance of DPS is growing because of the increase in the number of offshore construction sites requiring DPS for their operations (Mehrzadi et al. 2020). Over the last four decades, dynamic positioning (DP) in deep water has been used in the marine sector, oil and gas industries, and military services in many tasks such as drilling, oil and gas floating production platform, cable, and pipe laying, docking and towing, firefighting, supply, search and rescue, surveying, and mobile offshore bases (MOB). Each of these operations benefits from a DP system’s ability to include precise position-keeping, freedom from the restrictions of mooring spread systems, the ability to move quickly from one site to another, and track-keeping capabilities (Elkafas et al. 2021; Mahfouz 2007).

title: Effect of solid rubber fenders on the structural damage due to collisions between a ship-shaped offshore installation and an offshore supply vessel
Conversion and Customization of Conventional Platform Support Vessel into Well Stimulation Offshore Vessel; A Case Study from UAE Offshore
abstract: Offshore well stimulation is a critical and sophisticated operation in the oil and gas industry. It involves injecting various fluids and chemicals into wells to improve their production rates. These operations are complex, costly, and require meticulous planning and execution. A significant part of this planning involves ensuring that the necessary equipment and resources are available and effectively deployed. The focus of this paper is the conversion and customization of a conventional platform support vessel (PSV) into a well-stimulation offshore vessel. This case study, set in the UAE offshore, explores the detailed process, challenges, and results of this conversion. The primary objective was to create a vessel capable of supporting large-scale well stimulation operations, ensuring safety, efficiency, and cost-effectiveness. The offshore environment in UAE presents unique challenges due to its remote locations and the harsh marine conditions. Efficient well stimulation operations in such settings require vessels that are robust, reliable, and equipped with advanced technology to handle the demanding tasks. The conversion of a PSV into a well-stimulation vessel offers a practical solution, leveraging the existing capabilities of PSVs and enhancing them with specialized equipment and modifications.

Advancing Sustainable Marine Transportation: Offshore Floating Electric Vessel Charging Stations
venue: International Journal of Sustainable Energy Planning and Management
abstract: The feasibility analysis of offshore floating charging stations (FCS) incorporating renewable energy sources (RES) in India and around the world presents a promising and pioneering solution to meet the emerging demands of maritime transport systems for sustainable development. The global shift towards sustainable transportation supports the increasing adoption of electric vessels (E-vessel), which forces the inclusion of innovative solutions for their reliable operation. This study includes a feasibility analysis of FCS combined with an energy management system for reliable operation. A real-time analysis was conducted at an offshore location in the Arabian Sea, near Gujrat, India, to assess the operational and implementation possibilities of FCSs in India, especially in the Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ). An appropriate energy management system in the FCS tackles E-vessel demand changes, real-time variations in RES, and energy flow balance with reduced reliance on backup energy systems. The findings demonstrated a reduction of 70.2% in the backup energy requirement for the FCS, and the energy management system ensured that the FCS had an immense improvement in excess RES support to meet additional E-vessel demands. This paper also included a comparative analysis between an offshore location in India and one in Europe. This study underscores the potential of FCS to enhance the adoption of E-vessels in India’s and global marine transportation.

title: Branch-and-Price for Clash-Free Periodic Supply Vessel Planning Problem with Split Delivery and Variable Service Time
abstract: Efficient scheduling and routing of vessels is crucial in the oil and gas industries. In this paper, we consider a periodic supply vessel planning problem in which the weekly demands at multiple offshore facilities are satisfied with a fleet of heterogeneous vessels. Preemptive service at the base, variable service at facilities, and split delivery are allowed. The objective is to find the optimal fleet composition and weekly trips for vessels that minimize the total travel and fixed costs. The scheduling challenge is modelled by an arc-flow, path-flow, and set-partitioning formulations. For the first time in the literature of periodic supply vessel planning problem, we propose a branchand-price algorithm. Simulation results for the North West Shelf project in Australia show that the proposed approach can generate high-quality solutions to large, industrial-scale problem instances.

title: Hydrodynamic optimisation of a multi-purpose wind offshore supply vessel
A Global Operability Index for an Offshore Vessel
abstract: Abstract For the operability evaluation of an offshore unit, it is usual to adopt specific working limiting criteria dealing with ship motions and accelerations. These criteria given by operators reflect the ability of the vessel (or crew) to accomplish a precise target in an operative scenario with different meteorological conditions. However, an offshore vessel needs also to keep a determined position and heading during working operations. That means designers or operators have to consider criteria associated both with seakeeping and station keeping to evaluate the effective operability of the vessel. Traditionally, early design stage operability analyses do not combine seakeeping and station keeping predictions, which are referring to different working environments. Here, an innovative procedure allows to evaluate the joint operability of an offshore unit, adopting scatter diagrams for local environmental conditions. The method has been applied on a Pipe-Laying vessel, assessing the global operability for different areas of commercial interest.

title: CFD simulation of the passing vessel effects on moored vessel
Motion Planning, Guidance, and Control System for Autonomous Surface Vessel
venue: Journal of Offshore Mechanics and Arctic Engineering
abstract: Abstract This paper presents a motion planning, guidance, and control system for an autonomous surface vessel in a practical maritime environment. The motion planning algorithm is based on the angle-guidance fast-marching square method (AFMS), and the guidance system is based on the line-of-sight (LOS) trajectory tracking algorithm. To validate the motion planning algorithm, numerical simulations were carried out to compute the optimal path in a static environment including various obstacles. The guidance and control system were tested with an autonomous surface vehicle (ASV) tracking a pre-established trajectory including static obstacles. The autonomous surface vehicle is a self-propelled scaled ship model of 2.5 m equipped with sensors and actuators, inertial measurement unit (IMU), global positioning system (GPS), propulsion direct current (DC) motors, and wireless communication. From the experiments and numerical simulations, a good agreement was found.

title: Lifting simulation of an offshore supply vessel considering various operating conditions
abstract: Recently, an offshore support vessel is being widely used to install an offshore structure such as a subsea equipment which is laid on its deck. The lifting operation which is one of the installation operations includes lifting off, lifting in the air, splash zone crossing, deep submerging, and finally landing of the structure with an offshore support vessel crane. There are some major considerations during this operation. Especially, when lifting off the structure, if operating conditions such as ocean environmental loads and hoisting (or lowering) speed are bad, the excess of tension of wire ropes of the crane and the collision between the offshore support vessel and the structure can be occurred due to the relative motion between them. To solve this problem, this study performs the lifting simulation while the offshore support vessel installs the structure. The simulation includes the calculation of dynamic responses of the offshore support vessel and the equipment, including the wire tension and the collision detection. To check the applicability of the simulation, it is applied to some lifting steps by varying operating conditions. As a result, it is confirmed that the conditions affect the operability of those steps.

title: Beyond Vessel Motion: Direct Response Forecasting for Safer Offshore Lifting
abstract: Abstract Offshore lifting operations are frequently constrained by conservative pre-operation assumptions. These assumptions manage uncertainty but often reduce operability, increase waiting on weather, and underutilize vessel time. This paper presents a response-based forecasting approach for offshore lifting operations that integrates automated time-domain analysis with real-time environmental measurements and short-term forecasts within the ANALYSE. Lift framework. Unlike conventional methods that primarily screen operations using vessel motion metrics, the proposed approach evaluates the lifting system response directly, using governing quantities such as crane wire tension, crane tip motion and velocity, and rigging loads. The methodology covers both pre-operation planning and execution-phase decision support through continuously updated response forecasts. A demonstrator case study shows that headings that minimize vessel motions do not necessarily minimize critical lifting responses, and that direct response evaluation can identify safe execution headings and windows that are missed by motion-based screening. The work indicates that response-based forecasting can reduce unnecessary conservatism while maintaining or improving safety margins and substantially reduce manual analysis effort by automating repeated reassessments.
